idiom_name: defer in the acquire-check-defer idiom, optionally merging the teardown error into a named result
implementation_notes: Go's defer statement pushes the call onto the function's list and runs it when the function returns - on a normal return, during a panic, or when runtime.Goexit runs - so the pairing is written where the resource is acquired instead of in a separate wrapper method. What replaces the Smalltalk block is that statement plus an ordinary function boundary: when several callers should share one policy, write a plain function that opens, defers the close and takes the body as a func parameter, as in the sketch. Use defer directly when the resource belongs to the function doing the work; use the closure-taking wrapper for shared policy (retry, metrics, file locking) and when the teardown error must not be dropped.
pitfalls: A defer inside a loop runs when the enclosing function returns, not when the iteration ends: close in a per-iteration closure or move the body into a helper function, or every resource stays open until the loop finishes.
Deferring before checking the acquisition error calls the teardown on a nil or zero value; acquire, check the error, then defer.
Deferred calls run on panic but not when the program exits through os.Exit, and a deferred function can still modify a named result - keep cleanup logic short and do not hide meaningful work in it.
The teardown error is silently discarded unless the wrapper merges it into a named result or joins it explicitly.
